title: Fine-Tuning Transformers and PEFT/LoRA
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Fine-Tuning Transformers and PEFT/LoRA ##### ₹4.2 lakh, or one ₹90 GPU-hour A legal-tech startup in Pune needed a model that could draft clause summaries in Indian contract language — a domain where GPT-4 was competent but expensive at their volume, and where a general open model was noticeably worse. Their first plan was full fine-tuning of a 13B model. The arithmetic was discouraging: 13B parameters × 16 bytes per parameter for weights, gradients and AdamW state is 208 GB, plus activations. That means at least 4×A100-80GB, roughly ₹1,200/hour, for a multi-day run — around ₹4.2 lakh for the experimentation they expected to need. For a startup, that ends the conversation. They used QLoRA instead. The base model loaded in 4-bit (about 7 GB), trainable adapters totalled 0.18% of parameters, and the job ran on a single 24 GB RTX 4090 for 6 hours. Cost: under ₹1,000. The resulting model beat the base model by a wide margin on their internal evaluation and matched their full-fine-tune pilot within noise. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning is not a compromise you accept under constraint. For most adaptation tasks it is simply the right method. ##### Why full fine-tuning is so expensive For a model with P parameters, training in mixed precision with AdamW: | Component | Bytes/param | 7B | 13B | 70B | |---|---|---|---|---| | Weights (fp16) | 2 | 14 GB | 26 GB | 140 GB | | Master weights (fp32) | 4 | 28 GB | 52 GB | 280 GB | | Gradients (fp16) | 2 | 14 GB | 26 GB | 140 GB | | Adam m + v (fp32) | 8 | 56 GB | 104 GB | 560 GB | | **Total (excl. activations)** | **16** | **112 GB** | **208 GB** | **1120 GB** | Beyond memory, full fine-tuning has three operational problems: each task produces a full-size checkpoint (26 GB per customer is not a serving strategy), it is prone to **catastrophic forgetting** of general capability, and it needs far more data to avoid overfitting. ##### LoRA: the low-rank hypothesis Hu et al. (2021) started from an observation in the literature: the *update* learned during fine-tuning has low intrinsic rank. The pretrained model already contains the capability; adaptation nudges it along a small number of directions. So instead of learning a full update `ΔW ∈ ℝ^(d×k)`, factor it: ``` W' = W₀ + ΔW = W₀ + BA where B ∈ ℝ^(d×r), A ∈ ℝ^(r×k), r ≪ min(d, k) ``` Freeze `W₀` entirely. Train only `A` and `B`. For a 4096×4096 attention projection at r=16, that is 16.7M parameters replaced by 131k — a 128× reduction. ```python import torch, torch.nn as nn, math class LoRALinear(nn.Module): def __init__(self, base: nn.Linear, r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05): super().__init__() self.base = base for p in self.base.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False # freeze pretrained weights self.r, self.scaling = r, alpha / r self.lora_A = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(r, base.in_features)) self.lora_B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(base.out_features, r)) self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout) nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(self.lora_A, a=math.sqrt(5)) # B starts at ZERO -> BA = 0 -> model is bit-identical to base at step 0 def forward(self, x): return self.base(x) + self.drop(x) @ self.lora_A.T @ self.lora_B.T * self.scaling @torch.no_grad() def merge(self): """Fold the adapter into the base weight: zero added inference latency.""" self.base.weight += (self.lora_B @ self.lora_A) * self.scaling ``` Three design details carry all the weight: **B initialised to zero.** At step 0, `BA = 0`, so the model output is exactly the pretrained model's. Training starts from a known-good state with no shock. Initialising both matrices randomly injects noise into every layer and destabilises early training. **The `alpha/r` scaling.** It decouples the effective learning rate from the rank, so doubling r does not double the update magnitude. Convention is `alpha = 2r`. **Merging.** Because `W₀ + BA` is just a matrix sum, you can fold the adapter into the base weights after training. Inference then has **zero** added latency — unlike adapter layers, which add sequential computation to every forward pass. This is LoRA's decisive practical advantage. ```mermaid flowchart LR X[Input x] --> W[Frozen W0
4096 x 4096] X --> A[LoRA A
r x 4096 - trainable] A --> B[LoRA B
4096 x r - trainable] W --> S(( + )) B -->|scale alpha/r| S S --> Y[Output] ``` ##### QLoRA: 4-bit base, 16-bit adapters Dettmers et al. pushed further: quantise the frozen base model to 4 bits, and train LoRA adapters in bf16 on top. Since the base is never updated, quantisation error does not compound through training. Three innovations make it work: - **NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat):** a data type whose quantisation levels are the quantiles of a normal distribution — information-theoretically optimal for weights, which are approximately Gaussian. - **Double quantisation:** quantise the quantisation constants themselves, saving a further ~0.4 bits per parameter. - **Paged optimizers:** use NVIDIA unified memory so optimizer state pages to CPU RAM during memory spikes instead of OOM-ing. ```python from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, BitsAndBytesConfig from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, prepare_model_for_kbit_training import torch bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig( load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16, # dequantise to bf16 for the matmul bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.3", quantization_config=bnb, device_map={"": 0}, attn_implementation="flash_attention_2", ) model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model, use_gradient_checkpointing=True) peft_cfg = LoraConfig( r=32, lora_alpha=64, lora_dropout=0.05, bias="none", task_type="CAUSAL_LM", target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", # attention "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"], # AND the MLP ) model = get_peft_model(model, peft_cfg) model.print_trainable_parameters() # trainable params: 83,886,080 || all params: 7,331,340,288 || trainable%: 1.14 ``` Targeting the MLP projections as well as attention is worth stressing. The original LoRA paper only adapted `q_proj` and `v_proj`, and many tutorials copy that. QLoRA's ablations showed that **applying LoRA to every linear layer is the single most important factor** in matching full fine-tuning quality. The extra parameters are cheap; the quality difference is not. ##### Training with TRL ```python from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig cfg = SFTConfig( output_dir="out/clause-summariser", num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=4, gradient_accumulation_steps=8, # effective batch 32 learning_rate=2e-4, # 10-100x higher than full FT lr_scheduler_type="cosine", warmup_ratio=0.03, bf16=True, gradient_checkpointing=True, gradient_checkpointing_kwargs={"use_reentrant": False}, optim="paged_adamw_8bit", max_grad_norm=0.3, max_seq_length=2048, packing=True, # concatenate short examples, big speedup logging_steps=10, eval_strategy="steps", eval_steps=100, save_strategy="steps", save_steps=100, load_best_model_at_end=True, ) trainer = SFTTrainer(model=model, args=cfg, train_dataset=train_ds, eval_dataset=eval_ds, peft_config=peft_cfg) trainer.train() trainer.model.save_pretrained("out/adapter") # ~150 MB, not 14 GB ``` The learning rate deserves emphasis: LoRA wants **1e-4 to 3e-4**, roughly 10–100× higher than full fine-tuning's 1e-5. Using a full-fine-tuning learning rate with LoRA is the most common reason people conclude "LoRA does not work" — the adapters barely move. Also: mask the prompt tokens so loss is computed only on the completion. Training on the instruction text teaches the model to generate instructions, which is not what you want. TRL's `DataCollatorForCompletionOnlyLM` handles this. ##### The PEFT family | Method | Mechanism | Params | Inference cost | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---| | **LoRA** | Low-rank ΔW | 0.1–2% | Zero (merged) | The default | | **QLoRA** | LoRA on a 4-bit base | 0.1–2% | Zero (merged) | Largest memory saving | | **DoRA** | Decomposes into magnitude + direction | ~LoRA | Small | Better at low rank | | **Adapters** | Small bottleneck MLPs inserted per block | 1–5% | Added latency | Pre-LoRA standard | | **Prefix tuning** | Learned virtual tokens prepended to K,V | <0.1% | Consumes context | Fragile to train | | **Prompt tuning** | Learned soft embeddings at the input | <0.01% | Consumes context | Needs very large models | | **IA³** | Learned rescaling vectors on activations | <0.05% | Near zero | Extremely lightweight | Adapters (Houlsby et al.) came first but insert sequential layers, so they add real inference latency and complicate tensor-parallel serving. Prefix and prompt tuning avoid touching weights entirely but eat context window and are notoriously sensitive to initialisation. LoRA won because it is the only one that is both expressive and free at inference. ##### Choosing what to fine-tune — and whether to at all Ask these in order: 1. **Can prompting solve it?** Few-shot examples cost nothing and ship in an hour. 2. **Is it a knowledge problem?** Then it needs RAG, not fine-tuning. Fine-tuning teaches *behaviour, format and style*; it is a poor and expensive way to inject facts, and it will hallucinate confidently about anything adjacent. 3. **Do you have 500+ high-quality examples?** Below that, fine-tuning mostly overfits. Quality beats quantity decisively — 1,000 carefully curated examples beat 50,000 scraped ones. 4. **Is the base model close?** If it is far off, no adapter will bridge the gap; pick a better base. When you do fine-tune, hyperparameters in order of impact: target modules (all linear layers), then rank (8 for style, 16–32 for most tasks, 64+ for teaching a genuinely new skill), then learning rate, then epochs (2–3; more overfits). ##### Serving adapters The operational payoff arrives at serving time. A 150 MB adapter per customer instead of a 14 GB model means you can hold the base model in GPU memory once and hot-swap adapters per request. vLLM, LoRAX and TGI all support multi-LoRA serving, routing each request to its tenant's adapter with a single shared base. That is how a small team serves 50 customer-specific models on one GPU. ##### Common mistakes - Using a full-fine-tuning learning rate (1e-5) with LoRA and seeing no learning. - Targeting only `q_proj` and `v_proj` because the original paper did. - Fine-tuning to inject facts, when RAG was the correct tool. - Not masking prompt tokens, so the model learns to write instructions. - Forgetting `prepare_model_for_kbit_training`, leaving norm layers in an unstable dtype. - Rank 256 on 800 examples — vastly overparameterised, instant overfitting. - Merging a QLoRA adapter into the 4-bit base and losing quality; dequantise to fp16 first, then merge. - Adapter trained with one chat template, served with another. - No held-out evaluation, so "it looks better" is the entire validation. - `use_reentrant=True` gradient checkpointing silently breaking with PEFT. ##### Hands-on Fine-tune a mid-sized open model with plain LoRA in bf16, then repeat with QLoRA 4-bit on the same data and hyperparameters. Record peak GPU memory, wall-clock time, and an evaluation score for both, plus a baseline of the untuned model. Then ablate `target_modules`: attention-only versus all-linear, at the same rank. The gap you measure is the most instructive number in this exercise. For the mini-project, fine-tune an open LLM on a domain-specific instruction dataset with QLoRA end to end: dataset construction with a consistent chat template, completion-only loss masking, packing, a held-out evaluation set scored with both an automatic metric and a small LLM-as-judge rubric, and an adapter saved and published to the Hub. Then demonstrate merge-and-serve — load the base, apply the adapter, merge, and measure that inference latency is unchanged versus the base model. Write your explanation of how LoRA reduces trainable parameters (with the rank arithmetic) and why 4-bit quantisation of a frozen base is safe when the adapters stay in bf16. ##### Key takeaways - Full fine-tuning costs ~16 bytes per parameter in optimizer state; LoRA trains under 2% of parameters and QLoRA cuts the frozen base to 4 bits. - Zero-initialised B means training starts exactly at the pretrained model, and merging means zero added inference latency. - Target every linear layer, not just attention — it is the biggest single quality lever in PEFT. - LoRA needs a 10–100× higher learning rate than full fine-tuning; this trips up most first attempts. - Fine-tune for behaviour and format; use RAG for knowledge. Choosing the wrong one wastes the whole budget.
practical_task_reference: Fine-tune a mid-sized LLM with LoRA using Hugging Face PEFT, then repeat with QLoRA (4-bit) and compare memory usage and quality.
mini_project_reference: Fine-tune an open LLM on a domain-specific instruction dataset with QLoRA, evaluate it, and package the adapter for reuse.
assignment_reference: Explain how LoRA reduces trainable parameters and why QLoRA enables fine-tuning large models on limited hardware.
